config.title: Lippincott Micro Ch4 - Parasitology (JeffMD GI relevant)
config.subtitle: Parasitology questions sourced from Lippincott's Illustrated Q&A Review of Microbiology & Immunology

questions.stem: A child undergoes an appendectomy, and the pathologist identifies a parasite in the surgical biopsy (shown in the image). What is the most likely parasitic diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image shows a cross-section of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) in appendicular tissue — recognizable by its characteristic lateral alae and absence of internal nuclei typical of protozoa. Pinworms occasionally migrate into the appendix and are found incidentally in surgical specimens; whether they cause true appendicitis or are merely incidental is debated. Ascaris lumbricoides is a much larger roundworm and would appear massive in cross-section; hookworms reside in the small intestine and do not typically involve the appendix. Giardia and Entamoeba are protozoans and appear as single cells, not multicellular cross-sections.
keypoints: ⭐ Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) is the most common intestinal nematode in the US; spread by fecal-oral ingestion of embryonated eggs
⭐ Diagnosis: cellophane tape ('Scotch tape') test applied perianally in the morning before bathing — eggs are deposited at night
Pinworm may be found incidentally in appendectomy specimens — cross-sections show lateral alae and lack nuclei of protozoans
Treatment: pyrantel pamoate, albendazole, or mebendazole; repeat dose in 2 weeks to prevent reinfection
questions.imageAlt: Histological cross-section of Enterobius vermicularis in appendicular tissue
questions.imageCaption: H&E cross-section of appendix showing Enterobius vermicularis with characteristic lateral alae

questions.stem: A medical student, who is completing a pathology rotation, is given an assignment to review the collection of parasite specimens taken from patients with gastrointestinal disease. On one of the slides, the label is faded and unreadable. Even so, the specimen (shown in the image) is well preserved and, according to the attending pathologist, easy to identify. What is the identification of this parasite?
questions.explanation: The image shows the scolex (holdfast organ) of Taenia solium — identifiable by its four muscular suckers and a rostellum (crown of hooks), earning it the name 'armed tapeworm.' The hooks distinguish T. solium from T. saginata, which lacks them ('unarmed'). Ascaris and Toxocara are roundworms with no scolex. Fasciola is a fluke and has oral/ventral suckers but no rostellum. Echinococcus granulosus produces protoscolices within hydatid cysts rather than a free scolex in the intestine.
keypoints: ⭐ Taenia solium ('pork tapeworm'): armed scolex — 4 suckers + rostellum with 2 rows of hooks; T. saginata is unarmed (no hooks)
⭐ T. solium causes TWO diseases: intestinal taeniasis (eating undercooked pork) AND cysticercosis/neurocysticercosis (ingesting T. solium eggs)
Scolex identification: T. solium = hooks; T. saginata = no hooks; Diphyllobothrium = bothria (grooves, no hooks)
Praziquantel is first-line for intestinal T. solium; neurocysticercosis requires albendazole + corticosteroids ± anti-seizure meds
questions.imageAlt: Microscopic image of Taenia solium scolex showing suckers and rostellum with hooks
questions.imageCaption: Taenia solium scolex: four suckers and hook-bearing rostellum (armed tapeworm)

questions.stem: A woman who emigrated from Asia undergoes a spontaneous abortion, and in the recovery room she passes numerous proglottids. The medical technologist injects one of the proglottids with India ink to delineate the uterus (shown in the image). How did she become infected with this tapeworm?
choices: Consumption of insufficiently cooked pork sausage
Fecal contamination of food or drink
questions.explanation: The India ink injection reveals a uterus with 15–30 lateral branches per side, diagnostic of Taenia saginata (the beef tapeworm); T. solium has only 7–13 branches. T. saginata is transmitted by eating undercooked beef containing the cysticercus (bladderworm) larval stage. The intermediate host is cattle, not pigs (which carry T. solium). Fecal-oral transmission of eggs causes cysticercosis (T. solium), not intestinal taeniasis. Sushi transmission applies to Diphyllobothrium (fish tapeworm).
keypoints: ⭐ T. saginata uterus: 15–30 lateral branches → beef tapeworm; T. solium: 7–13 branches → pork tapeworm (India ink technique distinguishes them)
⭐ T. saginata: cattle are intermediate host; humans acquire by eating undercooked beef with cysticerci
T. saginata causes only intestinal taeniasis (no cysticercosis in humans, unlike T. solium)
Treatment: praziquantel or niclosamide; both are highly effective
questions.imageAlt: India ink-injected Taenia saginata proglottid showing uterine branches
questions.imageCaption: Taenia saginata proglottid with India ink: 15–30 lateral uterine branches diagnostic of beef tapeworm

questions.stem: What is an appropriate therapy for the woman in the above case? (The patient has been identified as having a Taenia saginata intestinal infection.)
questions.explanation: Praziquantel is first-line therapy for intestinal cestode (tapeworm) infections including T. saginata and T. solium, working by causing spastic paralysis and tegumental disruption of the worm. Chloroquine is an antimalarial. Ivermectin is used for filarial nematode infections (e.g., onchocerciasis, strongyloidiasis). Metronidazole targets anaerobic bacteria and select protozoa (Giardia, Entamoeba, Trichomonas) but has no activity against cestodes. Piperazine is used for Ascaris and Enterobius infections, not tapeworms.
keypoints: ⭐ Praziquantel: first-line for all cestode (tapeworm) AND trematode (fluke) infections — causes Ca²⁺ influx → spastic paralysis
⭐ Niclosamide is an alternative for intestinal tapeworms (inhibits oxidative phosphorylation in worm mitochondria)
Metronidazole covers: Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Trichomonas, C. difficile, anaerobes — NOT helminths
Mnemonic: PraziQUANtel = kills QUANtity of worms (tapeworms + flukes)

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman in Finland suffers from a macrocytic anemia. Her history is significant for frequent consumption of pickled fish. A stool sample reveals parasite ova like the one shown in the first image. Upon treatment, she expels a tapeworm similar to the stained specimen shown in the second image. With which tapeworm was she most likely infected?
questions.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum (broad fish tapeworm) is endemic to Finland and Scandinavia and is acquired by eating raw or insufficiently cooked freshwater fish. It uniquely causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia by competing with the host for vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum. The diagnostic egg is operculated (has a lid) with a small anopercular knob at the opposite pole. The scolex has bothria (elongated grooves) rather than suckers or hooks. No other tapeworm listed causes B12 deficiency.
keypoints: ⭐ Diphyllobothrium latum: only tapeworm causing megaloblastic anemia via vitamin B12 competition — scolex has bothria (no hooks/suckers)
⭐ Egg ID: operculated egg with prominent anopercular knob — found in stool; acquired from raw freshwater fish (pike, salmon, trout)
Endemic: Scandinavia, Finland, Great Lakes region, Japan; increasingly found in sushi consumers worldwide
Treatment: praziquantel; distinguish from other tapeworms — T. saginata/solium have suckers; Echinococcus produces hydatid cysts
questions.imageAlt: Diphyllobothrium latum operculated egg with anopercular knob
questions.imageCaption: D. latum egg: operculated with anopercular knob (characteristic of broad fish tapeworm)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old patient — a daughter of a migrant farm laborer — experiences onset of epileptic seizures. The family has recently arrived in the United States from Mexico. A few pea-sized lipomalike lesions are undeniably palpable in her subcutaneous tissue of her torso and limbs. Excision of two of these lesions reveals parasites (shown in the image). These parasites are active when placed in warm saline. MRI demonstrates similar lesions in the CNS, and an immunoblot assay is positive for the suspected parasitic disease. Of interest is the discovery of taeniid ova in the stool of her father. Which parasite is most likely the cause of the child's illness?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture — new-onset seizures in a child from Latin America with palpable subcutaneous cysticerci and CNS lesions — is classic neurocysticercosis caused by the larval stage (cysticercus) of Taenia solium. The child acquired this by ingesting T. solium eggs (fecal-oral route) from her father, who is presumably the adult tapeworm carrier. Echinococcus forms large fluid-filled hydatid cysts (not small mobile ones). T. saginata does not cause cysticercosis in humans. Toxocara causes visceral/ocular larva migrans, not cysticercosis. Onchocerca causes river blindness via filarial worms.
keypoints: ⭐ Neurocysticercosis = most common cause of new-onset seizures in immigrants from Latin America/Asia/Africa; caused by T. solium EGGS (not pork)
⭐ Distinguish: eating undercooked pork → intestinal taeniasis; ingesting T. solium eggs (fecal-oral) → cysticercosis
Diagnosis: MRI/CT (ring-enhancing lesions), immunoblot (most specific serology), direct visualization of cysticerci in biopsy
Treatment: albendazole + corticosteroids (anti-inflammatory) + anti-epileptics; praziquantel is an alternative cestocidal agent
questions.imageAlt: Excised cysticerci (bladderworms) from subcutaneous tissue — Taenia solium larvae
questions.imageCaption: Cysticerci (T. solium bladderworms) excised from subcutaneous lesions; mobile when placed in warm saline

questions.stem: What was the probable source or vehicle of infection for the child in the above case? (The child has been diagnosed with cysticercosis caused by Taenia solium.)
choices: Drinking fecal contaminated water at the farm labor camp
questions.explanation: Cysticercosis is acquired by ingesting Taenia solium eggs, not the cysticerci in pork. Since the child does not harbor the adult tapeworm herself, autoinfection is excluded. Her father, who carries the adult tapeworm (evidenced by taeniid ova in his stool), is the likely egg source — eggs contaminating salad or other raw foods are the most probable vehicle. T. solium eggs are immediately infective when passed in feces and require no soil development. Consuming undercooked pork leads to intestinal taeniasis (adult worm), not larval cysticercosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Cysticercosis source: T. solium EGGS via fecal-oral route (contaminated vegetables/water/unwashed hands), NOT undercooked pork
⭐ The adult tapeworm carrier in the household is the critical epidemiologic link — eggs passed in feces contaminate the environment
Autoinfection can occur in the tapeworm carrier themselves (reverse peristalsis → eggs reach stomach → hatching → cysticercosis)
T. solium eggs are immediately infective; no soil embryonation needed (unlike Ascaris)

questions.stem: Over a 1-week period, several elementary age children, who are involved in a summer camp in the Pocono Mountains of Pennsylvania, contract a gastrointestinal illness (i.e., they all exhibit similar manifestations like painful bloating and the passage of loose stools). A common microbe is present in fresh stool smears (example shown under oil immersion). Of the following means of transmission, which one is the most likely way each of these children became infected?
choices: Breathing (and swallowing) dust laden with bird droppings
Drinking contaminated lake or stream water
Eating rare or insufficiently cooked hamburger
Eating salad that contains dandelion flowers grown in nature
Poor hygiene practice of urinating while wading in streams
questions.explanation: The image shows Giardia lamblia trophozoites and cysts — the most common parasitic cause of waterborne diarrheal outbreaks in the United States. Giardia is transmitted predominantly by ingesting the cystic stage in contaminated water sources such as mountain streams or lakes (classic setting: campers and hikers). Bloating, flatulence, and greasy stools without blood characterize giardiasis. Foodborne transmission is possible but far less common than waterborne. Airborne transmission applies to fungal spores (histoplasmosis), not Giardia. Urinating in water is nonsensical as a mechanism for this intestinal infection.
keypoints: ⭐ Giardia lamblia: #1 waterborne parasitic diarrhea in the US — cysts survive chlorination; found in mountain streams (hikers/campers at risk)
⭐ Classic presentation: explosive, malodorous, greasy/fatty stools (steatorrhea), bloating, flatulence — NO blood (non-invasive)
Trophozoite: pear-shaped, 2 nuclei ('owl-eye'), ventral adhesive disc — attaches to small intestine mucosa
Diagnosis: stool O&P (cysts/trophs), stool antigen ELISA (most sensitive); Treatment: metronidazole or tinidazole
questions.imageAlt: Oil immersion stool smear showing Giardia lamblia trophozoites and cysts
questions.imageCaption: Giardia lamblia in stool smear: pear-shaped trophozoites with paired nuclei and oval cysts

questions.stem: A number of orphan children from a Third World nation are evaluated for failure to thrive. Some of these children present with debilitating parasitic diarrhea (representative stool sample shown in the image) and exhibit signs of malabsorption. Which of the following microbial virulence-producing attributes most accurately explains the pathology of this parasitic disease?
choices: Heavy parasite burden covering the epithelial surface of the duodenum
Lysis of the epithelial lining in the colon, resulting in blood in the stools
Massive infections, resulting in intestinal blockage and peritonitis
Perforation of the small intestine and hepatic abscess formation
questions.explanation: The image shows Giardia lamblia trophozoites and cysts. Giardia is a non-invasive protozoan that attaches to the duodenal and jejunal epithelium via its ventral adhesive disc. In heavy infections, the sheer number of organisms physically blankets the absorptive surface, mechanically interfering with digestion and fat absorption — causing steatorrhea and malabsorption. Giardia does not lyse epithelial cells (no blood in stools), does not cause iron-deficiency or macrocytic anemia directly, and does not perforate the intestine or form liver abscesses (those features belong to E. histolytica).
keypoints: ⭐ Giardia pathogenesis: mechanical obstruction of absorptive surface by massive trophozoite burden — NOT tissue invasion
⭐ No blood in stools = non-invasive (contrast: E. histolytica, Trichuris, hookworm all cause bloody stools)
Malabsorption: steatorrhea (fat), fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) deficiency — failure to thrive in children
Ventral adhesive disc = virulence factor allowing firm mucosal attachment; cysts are the infective/environmentally resistant stage
questions.imageAlt: Stool preparation showing abundant Giardia lamblia trophozoites causing malabsorption
questions.imageCaption: Giardia lamblia: heavy trophozoite burden in stool — mechanical interference with duodenal absorption

questions.stem: A missionary returns home from South America because of health problems. Principally, the patient is suffering from weeks of acute colitis. The diarrheic stool sample submitted for analysis is positive for occult blood, trophozoites with ingested erythrocytes (shown in the first image), and quadrinucleate cysts (shown in the second image). Based on these clinical findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of bloody diarrhea, trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells (erythrophagocytosis), and quadrinucleate cysts in stool is pathognomonic for Entamoeba histolytica. Erythrophagocytosis by trophozoites is the hallmark distinguishing pathogenic E. histolytica from morphologically identical but nonpathogenic E. dispar. Balantidium coli has a macronucleus and is associated with pig exposure. Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora cause watery (non-bloody) diarrhea and produce oocysts, not trophozoites. Giardia is non-invasive and never ingests RBCs.
keypoints: ⭐ E. histolytica hallmark: trophozoites with ingested RBCs (erythrophagocytosis) in bloody stool — distinguishes pathogenic from E. dispar
⭐ Quadrinucleate cyst = infective stage of E. histolytica; trophozoite = invasive stage causing flask-shaped ulcers in colon
Extraintestinal complication: amebic liver abscess (right lobe, single, 'anchovy paste' contents) — hepatoportal spread
Treatment: metronidazole (for invasive disease) + luminal agent (iodoquinol or paromomycin) to clear cysts
questions.imageAlt: Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite with ingested erythrocytes (erythrophagocytosis)
questions.imageCaption: E. histolytica trophozoite: ingested RBCs visible within cytoplasm — diagnostic of pathogenic amebiasis

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child is observed repeatedly scratching herself around the anal canal. Distinctive microscopic eggs (shown in the image) are detected via the cellophane tape technique. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image shows the characteristic eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) — oval, flattened on one side (D-shaped or asymmetrically oval), measuring ~55 × 25 μm, containing a developing larva. The cellophane tape test applied to the perianal area in the morning (before bathing) is the diagnostic gold standard, as the female deposits eggs there nocturnally. Ascaris eggs are round with a thick, bumpy shell. Trichuris eggs are barrel-shaped with polar plugs. Strongyloides is diagnosed by finding rhabditiform larvae in stool. Trichinella larvae encyst in muscle.
keypoints: ⭐ Enterobius (pinworm) egg: D-shaped/asymmetrically oval, flattened on one side — detected by perianal cellophane tape test in the morning
⭐ Most common intestinal parasite in US school-age children; spreads by hand-to-mouth from perianal scratching (eggs infective in 6 hours)
Nocturnal perianal pruritus = classic presentation; household spread is common (treat entire family)
Treatment: pyrantel pamoate, albendazole, or mebendazole × 1 dose, repeat in 2 weeks
questions.imageAlt: Cellophane tape preparation showing Enterobius vermicularis eggs (D-shaped, flattened on one side)
questions.imageCaption: Enterobius vermicularis eggs via cellophane tape technique: asymmetrically oval with developing larva

questions.stem: An immigrant from eastern Asia develops a cholangiocarcinoma. A fecal sample shows evidence of a parasitic infection which the physician believes to be linked to malignancy. What did the specimen reveal that led to this conclusion?
questions.explanation: Clonorchis sinensis (Asian liver fluke) and Opisthorchis species are associated with cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) due to chronic biliary inflammation and carcinogenic bile acid metabolism. The fecal specimen would reveal small, operculated fluke eggs diagnostic of clonorchiasis. Ameba cysts (E. histolytica) cause liver abscesses, not cancer. Cryptosporidium oocysts are linked to biliary disease in immunocompromised patients but not cholangiocarcinoma. Flagellated protozoans (Giardia) infect the small intestine. Nematode larvae are not implicated in biliary malignancy.
keypoints: ⭐ Clonorchis sinensis: Asian liver fluke — chronic biliary infection → cholangiocarcinoma; also linked: Schistosoma haematobium → bladder SCC
⭐ Transmission: eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish (metacercariae); endemic to East/Southeast Asia
Egg ID: small, operculated, pear-shaped with shoulder (vs. D. latum: operculated + anopercular knob; vs. Paragonimus: flattened operculum)
Treatment: praziquantel; WHO classifies C. sinensis as a Group 1 carcinogen

questions.stem: Which of the following modes of transmission accounts for the development of neurocysticercosis in humans?
questions.explanation: Neurocysticercosis is caused by larval Taenia solium (cysticerci) developing in the human brain/CNS — a result of accidentally ingesting T. solium eggs from fecally contaminated food or water (fecal-oral route). Humans then act as an aberrant intermediate host. This is entirely different from intestinal taeniasis, which is acquired by eating undercooked pork with cysticerci. Bladderworms in raw beef refer to T. saginata, which does NOT cause human cysticercosis. Ascarid eggs from soil cause ascariasis (intestinal infection). Cyclospora/Toxoplasma do not cause neurocysticercosis.
keypoints: ⭐ Neurocysticercosis = fecal-oral ingestion of T. solium EGGS → larvae hatch, penetrate gut wall, migrate to CNS
⭐ #1 cause of new seizures in adults worldwide; T. solium EGGS cause cysticercosis; T. solium CYSTICERCI in pork cause intestinal taeniasis
MRI: ring-enhancing lesions ('Swiss cheese' or 'starry sky'), scolex visible — pathognomonic on imaging
Household tapeworm carrier is the epidemiologic source; food handlers with untreated taeniasis pose risk to others

questions.stem: A businessman who recently returned from a trip to Scandinavia is diagnosed with diphyllobothriasis based on positive stool findings. What is the most likely vehicle for infection in this case?
questions.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum is transmitted by eating raw or insufficiently cooked freshwater fish (trout, pike, salmon, perch) containing the plerocercoid (infective larval stage) in the fish muscle. The parasitethe broad fish tapeworm — is endemic to Scandinavia, Finland, and the Great Lakes region. Drinking water does not transmit tapeworm larvae (it can transmit Giardia/Cryptosporidium cysts). Raw hamburger transmits T. saginata and E. coli O157. Salad greens may transmit Cyclospora, Toxoplasma, or T. solium eggs. Soil/sewage exposure relates to geohelminths like Ascaris and hookworm.
keypoints: ⭐ Diphyllobothrium latum transmission: raw/undercooked freshwater fish (plerocercoid larva in flesh) — classic: sushi, gravlax, ceviche
⭐ Unique complication: megaloblastic anemia from vitamin B12 competition (worm actively absorbs B12 from ileum)
Tapeworm eggs in water do NOT cause D. latum infection — eggs must be ingested by copepods → fish → human (3-host life cycle)
Scandinavian + Great Lakes endemic; increasingly seen in sushi consumers globally

questions.stem: Several individuals present with explosive watery diarrhea, mild fever, and profound fatigue. Epidemiologically, the common link is the eating of imported salad greens. Acid-fast preparations of fresh stools reveal large oocysts. Furthermore, the illness responds to TMP–SMZ treatment. What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Cyclospora cayetanensis oocysts are acid-fast, larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts (8–10 μm vs. 4–6 μm), and uniquely respond to TMP–SMZ — a feature that distinguishes Cyclospora from Cryptosporidium, which does NOT respond to TMP–SMZ. Cyclospora is linked to foodborne outbreaks via imported fresh produce (raspberries, lettuce, cilantro, basil). Cryptosporidium also produces acid-fast oocysts and causes watery diarrhea, but is waterborne and TMP–SMZ resistant. Giardia produces cysts (not oocysts) and is not acid-fast. Blastocystis and Entamoeba are not acid-fast.
keypoints: ⭐ Cyclospora vs. Cryptosporidium: BOTH acid-fast oocysts, watery diarrhea — KEY DIFFERENCE: Cyclospora responds to TMP–SMZ; Crypto does NOT
⭐ Cyclospora oocysts (8–10 μm) are TWICE the size of Cryptosporidium (4–6 μm) — largest acid-fast intestinal coccidian
Outbreak clue: imported fresh produce (raspberries, lettuce) — Cyclospora; outbreak in immunocompromised via water — Cryptosporidium
Cyclospora causes prolonged, relapsing diarrhea with waxing/waning course; can last weeks if untreated

questions.stem: A child with a helminth parasite is found to be anemic. Which parasitic worm is linked to microcytic anemia in children?
questions.explanation: Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) causes iron-deficiency (microcytic, hypochromic) anemia by attaching to the small intestinal mucosa and ingesting blood — each worm consumes approximately 0.03–0.1 mL blood/day. Heavy infections, especially in children, lead to significant iron loss and anemia. The broad fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) causes megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia via B12 competition, not microcytic anemia. Pinworm and pork tapeworm do not cause significant anemia. Schistosomes cause anemia through egg-related inflammation and chronic blood loss (hematuria in S. haematobium), but microcytic anemia is the hookworm hallmark.
keypoints: ⭐ Hookworm = iron-deficiency (microcytic/hypochromic) anemia — worms attach to intestinal villi and suck blood continuously
⭐ D. latum (broad fish tapeworm) = megaloblastic (macrocytic) anemia — B12 competition, NOT iron deficiency
Ancylostoma duodenale (Old World) more pathogenic than Necator americanus (New World) — A. duodenale ingests 3× more blood
Hookworm transmission: filariform larvae penetrate bare skin (feet) from warm moist soil → Löffler syndrome (pulmonary) → intestine

questions.stem: A young child, who was adopted from an orphanage in Asia, routinely experiences loose stools. An abundance of microscopic worms (shown in the image) are noted in a fecal preparation smear. What is the correct diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of an abundance of rhabditiform larvae (not eggs) in a stool preparation is diagnostic of Strongyloides stercoralis. Unlike most intestinal nematodes (which are diagnosed by finding eggs in stool), Strongyloides is identified by its larvae — which hatch within the intestinal lumen and are passed directly. The key word 'abundance' of larvae indicates active infection. Hookworm, Ascaris, Enterobius, and Trichuris are all diagnosed by eggs in stool, not larvae. Strongyloidiasis is common in children from developing nations and orphanages.
keypoints: ⭐ Strongyloides stercoralis: ONLY intestinal nematode diagnosed by LARVAE in stool (rhabditiform larva), NOT eggs
⭐ Unique feature: autoinfection — larvae can reinfect host through intestinal wall or perianal skin → hyperinfection syndrome in immunocompromised
Transmission: filariform larvae penetrate skin from soil (barefoot exposure) — similar to hookworm; endemic in Southeast Asia, tropics
Treatment: ivermectin (first-line) or albendazole; must treat before immunosuppressive therapy to prevent fatal hyperinfection
questions.imageAlt: Fecal smear showing abundant Strongyloides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae
questions.imageCaption: Strongyloides stercoralis rhabditiform larvae in stool — larvae (not eggs) are the diagnostic finding

questions.stem: An 8-year-old child, who recently emigrated with the family from Central America, is taken to the emergency department because of a stomach ache that has persisted for about 24 hours. In fact, the mother indicates that the pain did not lessen even after the child vomited up two worms (shown in the image) the night before. The mother further indicates that for the past several weeks the child has had little desire to eat and often complains of diarrhea. Physical examination reveals that the pain is more pronounced in the right upper quadrant region and directly radiates to the scapular area of the back. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image shows large roundworms characteristic of Ascaris lumbricoides — the most prevalent intestinal helminth worldwide, infecting over 1 billion people. RUQ pain radiating to the scapula indicates biliary tract migration, a serious complication of ascariasis. Children from Latin America commonly harbor multiple worms. Vomiting up worms is pathognomonic. Strongyloidiasis presents with larvae in stool, not visible worms. Hemolytic uremic syndrome follows E. coli O157 infection with bloody diarrhea and renal failure. Amebiasis causes bloody diarrhea with trophozoites in stool, not worm expulsion.
keypoints: ⭐ Ascaris lumbricoides: largest intestinal nematode (15–35 cm); biliary migration → RUQ pain, cholangitis, pancreatitis
⭐ Geohelminth: eggs must embryonate in soil before becoming infective — transmitted via contaminated soil/water/food, NOT person-to-person
Pulmonary phase (Löffler syndrome): larvae migrate lungs → eosinophilia, cough, fleeting infiltrates (Loeffler syndrome)
Treatment: albendazole or mebendazole; heavy burdens in children can cause intestinal obstruction and malnutrition
questions.imageAlt: Large roundworms (Ascaris lumbricoides) expelled by child — 15–35 cm in length
questions.imageCaption: Ascaris lumbricoides worms: large roundworms that can migrate into the biliary tract causing RUQ pain

questions.stem: With reference to the above question, how did the child most likely become infected with Ascaris lumbricoides?
choices: Direct fecal contamination from a sibling
Eating raw or insufficiently cooked hamburger
Ingestion of contaminated soil or water
Walking barefoot on moist soil or grass
questions.explanation: Ascaris lumbricoides is a geohelminth — eggs passed in feces must first embryonate in soil (requiring warmth and moisture, ~2–4 weeks) before becoming infective. The unembryonated egg in fresh feces is not immediately infectious, so direct person-to-person fecal-oral transmission (choice A) does not readily occur. Ingesting contaminated soil or food/water containing embryonated eggs is the primary route. Walking barefoot describes hookworm and Strongyloides transmission (skin penetration by filariform larvae). Swimming in cercariae-infested water is how schistosomiasis is acquired. Raw hamburger transmits E. coli O157 and T. saginata.
keypoints: ⭐ Ascaris = geohelminth: eggs MUST embryonate in soil (2–4 weeks) before becoming infective — NOT immediately contagious person-to-person
⭐ Contrast with Enterobius (pinworm): eggs ARE immediately infective (within hours) — highly contagious person-to-person
Soil contamination with human feces (poor sanitation) → contaminated vegetables/water → ingestion of embryonated eggs
Global distribution: tropical/subtropical; most prevalent helminth — >1 billion infected worldwide

questions.stem: A flight attendant, who works trips to Latin America, presents with fever, right upper abdominal pain, and blood-streaked diarrhea. A stained sample under oil immersion reveals the diagnostic stage (shown in the image). If treatment were to be withheld, what would the flight attendant be in danger of developing?
questions.explanation: The image shows an Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite under oil immersion — the invasive stage of amebiasis. Without treatment, E. histolytica trophozoites can spread hematogenously via the portal vein to the liver, forming an amebic liver abscess (the most common extraintestinal manifestation). The abscess classically contains 'anchovy paste' material (liquefied hepatic parenchyma), is typically single and in the right lobe, and is diagnosed by serology and ultrasound. Aplastic anemia and bladder cancer are unrelated to amebiasis. Cholangiocarcinoma is linked to Clonorchis. Pancreatitis can complicate Ascaris biliary migration.
keypoints: ⭐ Amebic liver abscess: most common extraintestinal complication of E. histolytica — right lobe, single cavity, 'anchovy paste' contents
⭐ Pathogenesis: trophozoites invade colonic mucosa → portal circulation → liver; cysteine proteases + ROS cause tissue destruction
Diagnosis: serology (ELISA) highly sensitive; ultrasound shows hypoechoic lesion; stool exam often negative in abscess patients
Treatment: metronidazole (invasive disease) THEN paromomycin/iodoquinol (luminal agent) to clear cysts and prevent recurrence
questions.imageAlt: Oil immersion stained preparation showing Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite
questions.imageCaption: E. histolytica trophozoite under oil immersion — invasive stage; erythrophagocytosis may be visible

questions.stem: A nurse who works part time in an elementary school in rural southern Mississippi notes loss of appetite, weakness, and poor school performance in a boy. The child's weight is below the second percentile, and a low hemoglobin level is noted in the laboratory findings. Of note, the child lives in a rural setting without adequate toilet or latrine facilities and customarily goes barefoot. Parasite eggs are observed in the stool sample (shown in the image). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of rural southern US setting, going barefoot, iron-deficiency anemia (low hemoglobin), growth failure, and characteristic thin-walled oval eggs in stool points to hookworm disease (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus). Filariform larvae in warm, moist soil penetrate bare skin — so walking barefoot is the key risk factor. Hookworms attach to the small intestinal mucosa and chronically suck blood, causing iron-deficiency anemia, protein malnutrition, and developmental impairment in children. Ascaris eggs have a thick mammillated shell and do not cause significant anemia. Strongyloides is diagnosed by larvae (not eggs) in stool.
keypoints: ⭐ Hookworm = iron-deficiency anemia + soil-transmitted; risk factors: barefoot in warm moist soil, poor sanitation, rural southern US
⭐ Egg ID: thin-walled oval eggs with segmented embryo (4–8 cells) in stool — contrast with Ascaris (thick bumpy shell) and Trichuris (barrel with plugs)
Transmission: filariform larvae penetrate intact skin (feet) → bloodstream → lungs → swallowed → small intestine
Necator americanus (Americas/Africa) vs. Ancylostoma duodenale (Mediterranean/Asia) — A. duodenale more pathogenic
questions.imageAlt: Thin-walled oval hookworm eggs in stool specimen
questions.imageCaption: Hookworm eggs: thin-walled, oval, with embryonic cells — passed in stool; larvae penetrate bare skin

questions.stem: A young child who lives in a rural community in the Appalachia and who has been ill for 10 days presents with abdominal pain, anorexia, steatorrhea, and watery diarrhea. There is no indication of blood in the stool, but a fecal smear stained with trichrome reveals an abundance of cystlike structures like the one shown in the image. What is the agent responsible for the clinical manifestations?
questions.explanation: The trichrome-stained fecal smear shows Giardia lamblia cysts — identifiable by their oval shape, hyaline cyst wall, axonemes (median bodies), and up to 4 nuclei (though sometimes only 2 are visible in cross-section). Steatorrhea and malabsorption without bloody stools in a rural child strongly suggests giardiasis, likely from contaminated rural water. Cryptosporidium cysts are much smaller and acid-fast (not trichrome-positive in the same way). E. histolytica causes bloody diarrhea. ETEC causes watery secretory diarrhea without encysted forms. Rotavirus is a viral cause without protozoan cysts.
keypoints: ⭐ Giardia cyst: trichrome stain shows oval cyst with up to 4 nuclei, axonemes (median bodies), hyaline wall — diagnostic finding
⭐ Steatorrhea + non-bloody watery diarrhea + trichrome cysts = Giardia (malabsorption syndrome, not colitis)
Appalachian rural setting: contaminated well water and streams are common sources of Giardia cysts
Giardia cysts survive chlorination; killed by boiling, UV, and 1-minute iodine treatment — important for backpackers/campers
questions.imageAlt: Trichrome-stained fecal smear showing Giardia lamblia cysts with axonemes and nuclei
questions.imageCaption: Giardia lamblia cyst under trichrome stain: oval shape, hyaline wall, axonemes, and up to 4 nuclei visible

questions.stem: In the summer, CDC investigates a series of outbreaks of cryptosporidiosis in upstate New York. The cluster of cases occurs in separate suburban communities, which are all upscale and feature a complete range of city services (e.g., sewage, water, and trash collection). Which of the following is the most plausible source of transmission for these outbreaks?
choices: Inhalation of dust seeding with bird droppings
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium parvum primarily infects livestock (cattle, sheep), and its oocysts can contaminate drinking water supplies when flooded stockyards or agricultural runoff contaminates municipal water sources. This explains outbreaks in otherwise well-serviced upscale communities that share a common water source. The 1993 Milwaukee outbreak (400,000 ill) is the classic example of Cryptosporidium entering a municipal water supply. Critically, C. parvum oocysts are highly resistant to standard chlorine disinfection. Bird-mosquito transmission is the West Nile virus cycle. Person-to-person spread is possible but doesn't explain simultaneous multi-community outbreaks.
keypoints: ⭐ Cryptosporidium parvum: chlorine-RESISTANT oocysts — standard municipal water treatment is INEFFECTIVE; requires filtration or UV treatment
⭐ Classic outbreak scenario: agricultural runoff/flooded stockyards → municipal water supply → large-scale community outbreak
Especially severe in immunocompromised (HIV/AIDS with CD4 <100): profuse watery diarrhea, cholangiopathy — can be fatal
No reliable treatment (nitazoxanide has modest effect); immune reconstitution (ART) is key in HIV patients

questions.stem: An HIV-positive student is considering part-time work to help with living expenses. Of the following jobs, which would be the most suitable, especially when considering the potential for contracting cryptosporidiosis?
choices: Life guard at a public pool
questions.explanation: Cryptosporidium oocysts are transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated water, animal contact, or human fecal matter. An animal hospital (exposure to livestock feces), daycare (diaper changes, infected children), public pool (oocysts shed in fecal accidents, chlorine-resistant), and pet store (animal feces) all represent significant exposure risks. A print shop involves no animal or fecal exposure and carries no risk for cryptosporidiosis — making it the safest occupation for an immunocompromised individual who cannot afford severe infection.
keypoints: ⭐ Cryptosporidiosis risk occupations: livestock/animal handlers, daycare workers, healthcare workers, swimmers (chlorine-resistant oocysts)
⭐ Cryptosporidium oocysts are chlorine-resistant — public pools pose real risk after fecal accidents (oocysts persist hours)
HIV patients with CD4 <100: most vulnerable to severe/fatal cryptosporidiosis (profuse diarrhea, wasting, biliary involvement)
Infection control for immunocompromised: avoid contact with livestock, diapered children, and untreated recreational water
